title: Unfreezing the 1970s Street: How Austin, Minneapolis & the "Montana Miracle" Proved Building Drops Rents 18%
tagline: Ending arbitrary $60,000 parking-stall mandates, single-stair bans, and 1970s lot freezes—uniting Texas, Minnesota, and Montana reformers with mass-timber robotics to bring back $135,000 starter homes.
cynicBelief: Runaway $2,500 rents and four-lane asphalt strip malls are just inevitable laws of modern capitalism—and building new apartments only invites luxury gentrification that raises neighborhood prices even faster.
breakthroughCounter: Almost every U.S. neighborhood was legally frozen between 1950 and 1978 by arbitrary parking minimums ($30,000–$75,000 per concrete stall), single-stair bans, and duplex prohibitions. When Minneapolis (2040 Plan), Austin (parking repeal + HOME 3-homes-per-lot), and Republican-led Montana (2023 bipartisan duplex/ADU legalization) unfroze housing supply, Austin rents dropped 14%–22% in real terms and Minneapolis held 6-year rent growth to ~1% while median wages climbed over 20%.
socialNormShift: Cross-partisan coalitions of property-rights conservatives, climate urbanists, carpenters, and Habitat for Humanity abolish minimum parking mandates, legalize 6-story single-stair courtyard buildings and backyard cottages by-right, and pair flexible Tokyo-style zoning with factory mass-timber starter homes.

humanStory.protagonist: Elena Reyes (29, NICU Nurse & Fiddler) & Caleb Miller (32, HVAC & Mass-Timber Carpenter)
humanStory.snippet: After Austin repealed parking minimums and legalized three starter homes per lot, Elena's apartment rent fell $310/month at renewal before she bought a $168,000 sunlit mass-timber courtyard townhome on a former 18-car asphalt lot—while in Montana, Caleb built a by-right backyard cottage for his widowed mom in six weeks with zero zoning lawsuits.

quote.text: Minimum parking requirements subsidize cars, punish people who cannot afford cars, drive up the cost of every apartment, and pave over the very neighborhoods people love.
quote.author: Prof. Donald Shoup
quote.role: Distinguished Research Professor of Urban Planning, UCLA & Author of The High Cost of Free Parking
